description: We are a team of Networks and Cybersecurity Engineering students at Helwan National University, Egypt. We are passionate about space, AI, programming, and solving real-world problems. We value creativity, teamwork, and innovation. We welcome motivated members skilled in Python, AI, data analysis, UI/UX, and scientific research. Together, we aim to develop an innovative and impactful project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Next Best Test is a browser-based prototype that helps astronauts decide what to check when support from Earth is delayed. It displays simulated heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, and fatigue on an interactive 3D body map. When readings change, a Bayesian model weighs possible explanations, including a faulty sensor. It ranks follow-up checks by how much they could improve the crew’s decision per minute and stops recommending checks when the expected benefit is small.

During limited contact windows, Next Best Message gives critical alerts priority and selects the most useful evidence that fits the available bandwidth. NASA’s Inspiration4 blood panels illustrate how to compare measurements with personal preflight baselines. JPL Horizons provides the one-way Earth–Mars signal delay used in the demo.

Across 1,000 simulated cases, the adaptive approach averaged 2.8 minutes of crew time and matched the model’s reference action in 88% of cases. The fixed checklist averaged 17 minutes and matched it in 89%.
details:
The problem

On a long-duration mission, a crew may have to investigate a health reading before Earth can respond. Next Best Test helps the crew decide which reading to verify first, when to stop testing, and what to send during the next contact window.

How it works

The browser-based monitor displays simulated vital signs alongside personal preflight baselines. An interactive 3D body map lets the crew select a measurement and see its trend, source, and relevant checks. A Bayesian model updates the likelihood of explanations such as fatigue, low blood oxygen, or a faulty sensor as new evidence arrives.

The engine estimates how much each follow-up check could improve the choice of action and ranks checks by the expected benefit per crew-minute. In our demo, a high wearable temperature prompts a two-minute check with an independent thermometer. When that result confirms the elevated reading, the model stops recommending further checks and queues an alert for Earth.

Communication with Earth

Next Best Message applies the same principle to a limited communications link. Critical alerts go first. The remaining space goes to the evidence most likely to improve Earth’s assessment per byte. The prototype also demonstrates configurable sharing levels and integrity checks for received messages.

NASA data and development tools

The project uses NASA’s Inspiration4 blood count and metabolic panel datasets, OSD-569 and OSD-575, to show how preflight baselines help interpret postflight lab results. NASA JPL Horizons supplies the one-way Earth–Mars signal delay used in the scenario. We built the prototype with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, used Three.js to render HuBMAP reference anatomy, and used Python to prepare the NASA datasets.

Results and intended impact

Across 1,000 simulated cases, adaptive testing averaged 2.8 crew-minutes compared with 17 minutes for a fixed checklist. The recommended action matched the model’s reference action in 88% and 89% of cases, respectively. Selective messages averaged 190 bytes of payload compared with 10,269 bytes for sending all available evidence. These results show how the approach could save crew time and bandwidth under the simulation’s assumptions.
